body:
100 meters is the perfect combination of visual, motion, soundtrack, and story. As someone who watched hundreds of anime for more than 15 years, i could confidently say that is the most realistic motion that i've ever seen. In this movie, they use rotoscoping method as they film the actual people, for example, the professional runner, and then animate it. As a result, all characters are moving surprisingly naturally. None of them stay still even it's just a standing scene. This's how realistic it is.

It may start slow in the beginning. Even some scenes may make you think 'it's not that deep, it's just a 100 meters run', but as the time goes by, there are many morals of the story. This movie is not just a sport movie but rather the movie for people who just started the adulthood, or still lost on the way of living. It reflect on how each character copes with their dreams and expectations while reality may be cruel; and how to move forward on life. It makes you think on the purpose or worthiness of the things that you're doing. Whether 'is it worth to do all of this?' or 'should i just enjoy the experience as everyone is going to die anyway?'.. i feel like the this movie give plenty of rooms for interpretation the philosophy hidden therein. So the obtained moral may be different for each person.

The movie truly represents what the author try to tell us. The tensity when the run starts make me feel like all of the things that you've been done will be decided within 100 meters. The sound of breathing, feet on the ground, everything is just so real. I have nothing to complain about. It is truly worth watching in the cinema.

100 Meters is a movie which feels personal at a much much deeper level...it's animation, cinematography, background music and the questions it raises through it's dialogues, that too at various stages of life, are brilliant.

It's animation choices depicting the first taste of defeat and the moment you live to play that sport for are just magnificent. I just believe that it comes down to those 100 meters and that too only for 10 seconds that have an answer to anything.

Togashi and Komiya represent how two rivals truly are not hating on each other but appreciating the other to push their boundaries.

Surprisingly gripping, 100 Meters easily earns an 8/10. What could've been a simple sports story turns into something deeply immersive and emotionally charged. The rotoscope animation is stunning-every movement feels raw and real, pulling you right into the athletes' world. The visuals are matched by a rhythmic, pulse-pounding score that brings the sprint sequences to life. It's not just about racing-it's about struggle, ambition, and pushing past your limits.

There's a meditative beauty in the training montages and a real sense of tension before each race. The film dives into the psychology of competition in a way that feels grounded and human. Even if you're not a sports fan, the emotion behind each frame makes it hard to look away. It manages to be both poetic and adrenaline-fueled. By the end, you're left inspired-and maybe even a little breathless.

"When I run, it hurts, more than reality, so it distracts me."

Not interested in sports (running)? Doesn't matter - watch it anyway!

What may seem at first like a simple sports anime turns out to be a film with much more depth.

This film creates a unique character duality/dynamic: driven by the same sport, motivated differently, yet sharing the same goal - 100 Meters - the solution to all their problems.

(Recommendation: Ping Pong the Animation, if you enjoyed this film.)

On a technical level, it's equally impressive: The animation and art style feel fluid, like a fresh breeze. The music and sound are high-quality, always perfectly matching the mood.

One of the most striking moments:

(LIGHT SPOILER!) (The 100-Meter rain scene: rain fills the screen, blending colors into black, gray, and white, focusing on the characters' outlines and expressions - and on the tension before the race. A moment that visually shifts toward almost monochrome tones, making it an unforgettable and cinematically ambitious highlight.)

Why Do We Run?

In the end, it becomes clear that passion outweighs the obsession with winning - it's more than just a competition.

The film turns into a story about hope, joy, self-fulfillment, rivalry, and friendship.

I felt so free and inspired after watching 100 Meters.

I recently discovered this author through the anime *Orb: On the Movements of the Earth*, which absolutely blew me away with its depth and artistry. So, when I learned that another of his stories was being adapted into a movie, I was thrilled. This film dives into the profound question of what motivates people, centering on the 100 meter dash. It follows a main protagonist, a key supporting character, and a diverse group of athletes, each grappling with their personal drive to compete. True to this author's style, the story is steeped in philosophical undertones, which adds such rich layers to the narrative.

The movie itself was phenomenal. The visuals were stunning, with breathtaking use of rotoscoping in certain scenes that gave it an almost hand drawn feel which is a remarkable feat in today's animation landscape. Overall, I was thoroughly impressed with this standalone film and would absolutely watch it again. It's a must see for fans of thoughtful storytelling and striking visuals.
